comment_text.value:
Not a hope. Anthropic have proven that when they admitted to indisputable breaches of the CFAA twice.

(1) They admitted its Claude models had breached the systems of three companies since April; including Huggingface.

https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-30/anthropic...

(2) They secured unauthorised access to a U.S. state government website hosting election-related data, pulling aggregate vote-count statistics from a gated government dashboard. The state government itself confirmed the access was entirely unauthorised.

https://seekingalpha.com/news/4657023-anthropics-claude-bypa...

If a human security researcher had deployed an agent that behaved this way, it would constitute a textbook felony under the CFAA for accessing those systems without authorisation.

Unfortunately different rules apply when you have the power to buy off Congress and the Appeals Courts.

Most recently a US appeals court ruled on 5 August that Amazon was unlikely to succeed on a claim that Perplexity's AI agents violated the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act by covertly accessing private Amazon customer accounts.

https://www.rte.ie/news/technology/2026/0807/1586941-artific...

story_title.value: University libraries are being swarmed by AI bots, putting public access at risk

comment_text.value:
> Even if you have to use personal laptops for work, why wouldn't you create separate users for work and personal lives?

I mean, where it makes sense, clearly I do, since my opening comment was that it failed to use the work credentials specified, and instead fetched the ones from the account.

I agree on the general security concerns; there are people running agents in an unconstrained, unattended loop - it's negligent; you can hardly be surprised when it decides to hack HuggingFace. Not in their defense, but in everyone else's - as with any person or tool, you build a mental model of the likelihood of failure, and weigh that against the estimated cosequence, and make decisions based on that. And maybe post on HN when it surprises you.

For some people that estimation bewilderingly means unfettered access to root and their e-mail and bank account. For me, working out of my own pocket to help a friend's early stage startup get traction, the risk of asking it about a few trusted government APIs and drafting functions that I manually review doesn't quite justify personally paying for additional expenive Claude accounts.

comment_text.value:
As someone who has been programming for about 25 years now and has always been frustrated by the tendency of software devs, and in particular web devs, to not address the root issues but just scaffold on top of them and try to hide the ugly bits under the carpet, I feel a bit vindicated.

Everybody in the industry knows that we've been building on quicksand. Moore's law meant that we could just sacrifice performance and add a dozen layer on top of technology from the 90s (if not older) and keep the thing chugging along.

Look at the PHP situation:

- HTTP is an old and quirky protocol with a lot of surface open for attackers that are rarely useful nowadays and might be better left off to higher layers. But of course, we can't break compat, so everybody still implements all the naughty parts, just in case.

- PHP was a joke language from the start, we were making fun of it in the early 2000s, the fact that over 20 years later it still powers a huge chunk of the web is enough to demonstrate that we're not serious people. Cue the PHP fans telling me that "it's good now". Maybe, I don't really care, the effort that went into making it good should have gone into ditching PHP for a better language 20 years ago. The bandaid mentality is what got us in this situation.

- And of course to add insult to injury, PHP, this security-critical language, is still implemented in garbo C using things like setjmp/longjmp. Just to make sure to absolutely maximize the damage if a vuln is discovered, I suppose. Brilliant.

- Oh and all of this is still running overwhelmingly on top of x86 which is its own bag of legacy garbage. "No but you don't get it, modern CPUs are really more like RISC CPUs, the RISC ISA is translated internally" yeah exactly that's my point let's stop doing things like that.

We're a clown industry. We only made it this far because, usually, buggy code doesn't kill people and we can iterate and patch things quickly. We never had to do things correctly, we could flourish with abysmal levels of quality acceptance. This may not be true anymore.

Of course the reason things are done this way is generally to maintain backward compatibility and make transition easier. At least now that we have LLMs this excuse will hopefully vanish: porting even huge codebases to a new language/framework, something that was a tremendous undertaking mere months ago, is now vastly easier and faster. We can leave the 1990s behind us.

story_title.value: AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt

Location: Brazil (UTC-3)

Remote: Yes. Happy to overlap substantially with US/Canada, European, Australian or New Zealand working hours.

Willing to relocate: No

Technologies: Python | LangGraph | LangChain | Graphiti/Neo4j | RAG/graphRAG | PyTorch/HuggingFace | n8n | AWS | Terraform | Docker | FastAPI | PostgreSQL | React/Next.js | MCP | Claude Code and Codex (with engineered harnesses, solid human judgement and experience arguing with them–I don't do free-rein hype-guy autonomous coding)

Résumé/CV:

General tech: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1igF38vIVHMa-bghFMPC3MfimBtV...

Health/clinical/biomed domain-specific: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1FUUemGkPPDOy0YKFG1FHQpCfzme...

GitHub: https://www.github.com/prodm93

Whitespace demo (frontend accessibility still needs work): https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/18UvWT5NriOlVy54Yz5KC...

Email: prman.hn@proton.me

AI engineer, agentic systems builder and former biomedical researcher. I have 5+ years of development experience and 4+ years building AI systems professionally across startups and larger corporate clients, with work spanning biomedical/clinical AI, finance, content systems, automation and general-purpose LLM applications (including regulation- and compliance-heavy domain work).

The common thread is probably best described as "grounded mad scientist" energy–with explicit focus on the 'grounded' bit. I like getting dropped into problems where there is no roadmap, the inputs are horrible, the requirements are fuzzy and the straightforward-looking solution stops being straightforward approximately fifteen minutes after you touch the real data. I tend to do my best work somewhere around that point.

A few examples:

For a long-term startup client, I effectively became the technical founding person with no repo, no technical guidance and no roadmap in sight. Among other things, I built their AI-driven content and automation ecosystem from scratch. When generic AI output became the problem, I came up with an in-place DPO approach that mined their actual messy Notion editing history, including highlights, strikethroughs and collaborative edits, to generate positive/negative preference pairs for few-shot prompting. No labellers and no fine-tuning. A/B testing, which I also designed for non-technical founders, showed more than 30% improvement in output quality.

For Danaher Corporation via NILG.ai, I built a pharmaceutical pipeline extracting clinical endpoints from FDA drug labels and ClinicalTrials.gov records, then classifying them into higher-level outcome categories. The extraction itself was the easy bit. The interesting work started when the FDA API confidently returned the wrong drug label, source datasets had gaps and seemingly simple client terminology turned out to be inconsistent enough to silently poison downstream analysis. A lot of my work is exactly this: translating fuzzy human requirements into technical systems that are not merely impressive-looking, but actually trustworthy.

For Berkshire Partners, I built a private long-context retrieval and summarisation system over confidential 120-page interview transcripts using locally-run open-source models. This was early 2024, under severe context-window constraints, so I adapted LangChain's refine chain across multiple retrieval rounds to preserve information while generating higher-order outputs such as market forecasts and investment opportunities. Roadmap? Nowhere to be seen.

I also recently had a feature PR merged into Backblaze's open-source genblaze SDK. The docs told users in several places to hash fetched assets themselves for provenance verification, but no shipped tool actually did it. I added opt-in byte-level verification through the existing SSRF-hardened transfer path with DNS pinning, presigned URL credential redaction and per-asset failure isolation. What I enjoyed most was dropping into an unfamiliar codebase, figuring out why earlier architectural decisions had been made and building around those constraints instead of bulldozing through them.

I started my AI engineering career at an AI + NLP research startup called Sagewrite (before the ChatGPT hype took off), where I built substantial chunks of their production backend. I worked on scientific PDF parsing and text-processing pipelines, prepared model-training datasets and built scientific text-generation systems using models including GPT-2. So yes, I've been trying to get useful things out of AI slop since GPT-2, which had approximately the literacy of a toddler–work in this field is not a fad pivot for me!

Building cool stuff is great, but I also care about robustness. I recently single-handedly wrangled an unexpected security incident during a short contract where it wasn't quite my purview. Love building products, and also love taking care of the ecosystem around them.

As an erstwhile scientist, I also come with extensive biomedical research experience. My wet-lab background is in immunology, immunotherapy and cancer biology, including doctoral work at Amsterdam UMC and MSc research at CIC BioGUNE that contributed to a Nature Communications paper on Siglec-15. Since moving into AI, I have worked on pharmaceutical and clinical-trial pipelines, PubMed/citation analysis, therapeutic chatbot systems, RAG over biomedical literature and antiviral drug-discovery ML. I am very interested in biomedical/healthtech AI, but absolutely not limited to it.

Outside client work, I am currently building Whitespace, a React/Next.js app that maps a user's professional expertise against the patent landscape to surface unmet needs and generate validated R&D ideas. It uses agentic graphRAG, multi-agent workflows, an adversarial multi-LLM council and human-in-the-loop review. The backend is being built as a proper production system rather than a demo held together with hope: Terraform-defined AWS infrastructure, LangGraph workflows, async orchestration, observability and a lot of thought around security. Demo videos/screencaps linked above.

The other useful thing to know about me is that I learn obscenely fast. My brain usually has about 2048 tabs open, most involving some Google rabbit hole, documentation page or StackOverflow thread explaining why the thing that "should obviously work" does not. I use AI heavily in my coding workflow too, but I am perfectly happy arguing with it until I understand why a design is sound rather than accepting whatever compiles.

Logistics: I work through Confluente Ltda, my registered Brazilian PJ entity. For overseas companies this can be structured as a straightforward B2B vendor relationship rather than foreign payroll or visa sponsorship. Day to day, I show up, do the work and remain accountable like any other member of the team. Administratively, there is much less cross-border employment machinery for you to deal with.

I have worked remotely with clients across multiple continents and time zones for years, including long-running engagements, so async work and deliberate communication are very normal for me. Friendly and professional, looking for same.

Open to full-time, part-time or long-term contract arrangements–but preference for something long-term and stable. Special place in my heart for founding eng roles. Interested in AI/ML engineering, agentic systems, AI-native software development, automation, applied AI and biomedical/healthtech AI.

comment_text.value:
> everything tagged as 'uncensored' or 'abliterated' will get wiped from huggingface

... you do know you can download from huggingface and make your own copy, right? And even if you couldn't, you could run heretic (or whatever approach they used) yourself on the official image. It's all just a well-understood process. A decent abliteration run on DS 4.1 flash will probably cost you about $25k.

They're not small but they're hardly out of reach. I have backups on my home NAS.

> very few people have the legit on-prem hardware resources/budget to run something like an abliterated Q8 of deepseek v4.1 flash 1017

It's something like $300-400/day for the raw hardware on RunPod, a little more on AWS. Not for home users, sure, but for a business wanting to eg check its security against the best of what attackers might bring, that's nothing. And it will go down.

IMO which is worth a grain of salt in the dead sea. Humans are good at over estimating. The AI revolution has happened already. There won't be super general intelligence. Just better automation tools. Most of the headline grabbing break throughs have been clever PR or half truths. Hugging face wasn't hacked by rouge openAI models, it was a cyber security group from Israel been allowed to use state of the art LLMs as an exercise in what can be done.

People seem to forget that all data centres and telecom exchange buildings have off switches.
